description_full: BJ's Wholesale Club Holdings, Inc., together with its subsidiaries, operates membership warehouse clubs on the eastern half of the United States. The company offers groceries, fresh food, general merchandise, gasoline, and other ancillary services. It sells its products through its clubs; the BJs.com website; and its mobile app. The company was formerly known as Beacon Holding Inc. and changed its name to BJ's Wholesale Club Holdings, Inc. in February 2018. BJ's Wholesale Club Holdings, Inc. was founded in 1984 and is headquartered in Marlborough, Massachusetts.

CEO compensation is 7× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags moderate compensation governance risk (4/10).
financial_summary: BJ's Wholesale Club Holdings, I is a large-cap consumer defensive business with a $13.8B market cap on $21.5B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +4% over the past three years, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 26% against a 7% cost of capital — a 19-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat.

The business throws off $328M in free cash flow — roughly 2 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.78× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, leverage is comfortably conservative at 0.4× net debt/EBITDA, and interest coverage of 19× is fortress-like.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome, and profit capture is only 0.5× the fair share, suggesting no structural edge inside its industry.

sect: Its 4% operating margin is roughly in line with the Consumer Defensive median (7%).
It captures well under its share of sector profits (0.47x its revenue share).
It accounts for 0.6% of sector revenue and 0.3% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+1.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.07 across 172 companies in the universe; the top four hold 38% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares have drifted higher, up 8% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits near the top of its 52-week range, 3% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 31% and a beta of 0.41, it is more defensive than the market, though its beta has shifted (1y -0.86 vs 5y 0.23), so read it loosely.
Liquidity is deep, with about $168.1M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 24% in the 2020 crash and 25% in the 2022 bear market.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $85.23 (margin of safety -28%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 18%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $58.83 to $127 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Consumer Defensive peers: P/E 23.9 vs 18.5, EV/EBITDA 14.5 vs 10.3 and P/FCF 42.1 vs 16.0 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 57% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 2.4% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 4.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 20 covering analysts target $106 on average, 3% below the price.
prof: ROIC of 26% clears the cost of capital of 6.8% by 19pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have been steady (CV 0.25).
It converts 2% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: a Piotroski score of 7/9 and cash conversion of 1.78x.
ROE of 26% is amplified by 3.4x balance-sheet leverage (DuPont), so ROIC is the cleaner read on the business.
It spends 0.2% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: Leverage is conservative at 0.4x net debt to EBITDA ($46.2M of cash against $519.1M of debt), with interest covered 19.3x.
The current ratio of 0.75 means short-term liabilities exceed current assets.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.6% over 3 years and 6.8% over 5 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 64% of profits supports about 16.4% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded -12.8% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Forward indicators: a book-to-bill of 1.00, a backlog worth 0% of annual revenue and deferred revenue down 16%.
Capex runs 2.4x depreciation (3.3% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 8, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.6%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (22 sales, net $32.6M sold).
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (2.1% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 1.5% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
people: With about 35,000 employees, each generates about $613K of revenue, 1.2x the Consumer Defensive median, and productivity has risen 7.4% a year.
That works out to $9K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $4.2M (7x revenue per employee).
